claims.claim: Stars form when dense cores inside cold molecular clouds collapse under gravity; the collapsing object is a protostar until hydrogen fusion ignites in its core.
A star is born when nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium begins in its core; the ability to generate energy by fusion is what defines a star.
The main sequence, during which a star steadily fuses hydrogen into helium, is the longest and most stable phase of a star's life.
A one-solar-mass star such as the Sun remains on the main sequence for roughly 10 billion years; the Sun is roughly midway through that phase.

More massive stars are more luminous, burn their fuel much faster, and live much shorter lives: the most massive stars spend only a few million years on the main sequence, a star of about 0.4 solar masses can last roughly 200 billion years (longer than the current age of the universe), and a 15-solar-mass star lives about a thousandth as long as the Sun.

When core hydrogen is exhausted, a Sun-like star expands into a red giant and eventually sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving an Earth-sized white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy pressure that cools over billions of years.

Stars with initial masses up to about 8 solar masses (possibly as much as 10) can end their lives as white dwarfs; the Sun will probably lose about 45 percent of its initial mass and become a white dwarf of less than 1.4 solar masses.

Massive stars fuse progressively heavier elements up to iron; fusing iron consumes energy rather than releasing it, so the iron core collapses and the star explodes as a supernova that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy.

The collapsed core of a massive star becomes a neutron star (about 10 to 20 kilometers across, among the densest objects known, mostly neutrons) unless its mass exceeds about 3 solar masses, in which case nothing can stop the collapse and the remnant is a black hole, an object from which not even light can escape.

Stars manufacture nearly all elements heavier than helium: fusion builds elements up to iron inside stars, and elements heavier than iron are synthesized in supernova explosions, so the atoms in our bodies and planet were forged in stars (we are made of star stuff).
Material expelled by dying stars enriches molecular clouds and becomes incorporated into the next generation of stars, so stellar life cycles drive the chemical evolution of the universe.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The initial-mass boundaries between the white-dwarf, neutron-star, and black-hole end states are approximate and model-dependent rather than exact cutoffs.
positions: OpenStax 23.1: stars up to about 8 solar masses (possibly as much as 10) can shed enough mass to end as white dwarfs.
OpenStax 23.2: a supernova explosion requires a star of at least about 8 solar masses; the neutron-star upper mass limit is only about 3 solar masses.
OpenStax 24.5: if the collapsing core's mass is greater than about 3 solar masses, theory says nothing can stop the collapse to a black hole.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states these as approximate boundaries ('about', 'roughly') and frames the neutron-star-versus-black-hole choice in terms of the surviving core's mass rather than the star's initial mass, exactly as the sources do.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The mass-luminosity relation used to estimate main-sequence lifetimes is an approximation, not a universal law.
positions: OpenStax 22.1 states the observed lifetimes directly (1 solar mass about 10 billion years; 0.4 solar masses about 200 billion years; the most massive stars only a few million years).

The luminosity-proportional-to-mass-to-the-3.5-power scaling is a standard approximation; using it, a 15-solar-mass star lives about 11 million years, consistent with OpenStax's 'few million years' for the most massive stars.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson leads with the directly sourced lifetimes, presents the scaling as 'a useful approximation', and the worked example labels the arithmetic as approximate; the 15-solar-mass result (roughly 10 million years, about a thousandth of the Sun) was verified arithmetically.
